title: Everyone on the video call was fake
summary: A finance employee at Arup in Hong Kong was suspicious, until he saw the CFO and colleagues on a video call. All were deepfakes. He transferred 200 million Hong Kong dollars, about 25 million US dollars.
disclaimer: Interactive reconstruction: the messages are illustrative, the exact wording is not public. The facts in the timeline come from statements by Hong Kong police and Arup, as relayed by CNN and Insurance Business.

steps.narration: You work in finance at the Hong Kong office. An email arrives from the UK office.
steps.message:
Subject: Confidential transaction

We are preparing a confidential transaction. Please treat this as strictly confidential, details will follow on a video call.
steps.question: Your gut says: this smells like phishing. What do you do?

options.label: Join the video call, then I will know whether it is real
options.feedback: That is what the real employee did too: his doubts were right, but the call was made to dispel them.

options.label: Call the CFO on the known number before anything happens
options.feedback: Exactly. Your first feeling was right, and a call back through a known route takes two minutes.

steps.narration: On the video call you see the CFO and several colleagues you know. They look and sound as they always do.
steps.message: Thanks for joining so quickly. We need to send the payments to these accounts in Hong Kong today. You know how confidential this is.
steps.question: You can see and hear them, after all. What do you do?

options.label: They are all here, that is enough for me: I transfer
options.feedback: What you saw and heard was generated. According to the police, every person on the call was fake.

options.label: Hang up and check through the normal approval route and a known contact
options.feedback: Right. A face and a voice prove nothing today. The agreed process does.

timeline.what: A finance employee in Hong Kong first takes an email about a secret transaction for phishing. After a video call with the supposed CFO and colleagues he drops his doubts and makes 15 transfers totalling 200 million Hong Kong dollars.
Only a follow-up with the UK headquarters uncovers the fraud. Arup reports it to the police.
Hong Kong police make the case public without naming the company: every person on the call was fake.
Arup is revealed as the company and confirms that "fake voices and images were used". According to Arup, internal systems were not affected.

lesson: The employee was right, until the video call convinced him otherwise. When money is involved, it does not matter who you see, only whether you asked through your own, known route.

title: The 7,000 bitcoin theft
summary: In May 2019 attackers stole about 7,000 BTC from the crypto exchange Binance. They did not need a hole in the core code: over a long time they collected API keys and 2FA codes from users, among other things through phishing and malware.
disclaimer: Interactive reconstruction: the messages are illustrative. The facts in the timeline come from the public statement by Binance.

steps.narration: You trade crypto privately on a large exchange. The year is 2019.
steps.message:
From: support@binance-security.test
Subject: Unusual sign-in detected

Confirm your account within 12 hours or withdrawals will be locked.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Open the link and confirm the account
options.feedback: The attackers' first step is done: the copy captures your password and 2FA code.

options.label: Open the real site yourself using a bookmark
options.feedback: Exactly right. No warning on the real site: the email was fraud.

options.label: Delete the email and forget it
options.feedback: Your account is safe. Reporting it to support would have helped even more.

steps.narration: Someone in your crypto group shares a tool that supposedly shows you better prices.
steps.message:
Trading_Bot_Pro_Setup.exe
"Just enter your API key, it runs by itself!"
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Install it and enter the API key
options.feedback: Malware and a handed-over API key: attackers can now trade in your name.

options.label: Do not install it and warn the group
options.feedback: Strong. An API key is worth as much as your password, sometimes more.

options.label: Install it, but with a read-only key
options.feedback: Better, but the malware still runs on your computer and reads what you type.

steps.narration: The attackers wait patiently for the right moment. A notification reaches you.
steps.message:
New API key created.
Was this you?
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Ignore it, it will be fine
options.feedback: This is the moment that decides the damage: nobody reacted, and the attackers keep collecting.

options.label: Delete the key right away, change the password, inform support
options.feedback: Exactly. A quick report can make whole waves of attacks visible earlier.

timeline.what: According to Binance, the attackers collect user data such as API keys and 2FA codes through phishing, viruses and other attacks. They wait patiently.
About 7,000 BTC are withdrawn in a single transaction, then worth about 40 million US dollars. The transaction is structured so that it initially passes the alert systems.
Binance suspends deposits and withdrawals for a time and covers the loss from its SAFU security fund.

lesson: The most expensive attack did not begin in the code but with individual people. Every reported phishing email would have made the preparation more visible.
sources: Public statement by Binance on the security incident, May 2019

title: The 6 billion dollar job interview
summary: In October 2026 Binance lost about 6.3 billion US dollars, the largest crypto theft in history. It began with a tampered download and a job interview that never really existed.
disclaimer: Interactive reconstruction: the messages are illustrative, the facts in the timeline come from Binance's incident report as relayed by the media named below. The amount is reported differently (6.34 to 6.43 billion US dollars). Binance itself expressly says this was not "a simple phishing incident" but a multi-stage campaign.

steps.narration: June 2026. You are a DevOps engineer working on the wallets of a large exchange. You want to try a well-known AI tool and search for it online. It needs a package manager, and a matching result sits right at the top.
steps.message:
Ad · brew-install.test
Install Homebrew in one step
"Official installer for macOS"
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Trust the first result and run the installer
options.feedback: The attackers learn what you do and who else looks after the wallets. Binance detected the download and removed it, but the attackers kept that knowledge.

options.label: Get software only through the route your company has approved
options.feedback: Exactly. Search results and ads are no way to obtain tools for a computer with these rights.

steps.narration: September 2026. You are a software engineer. On a reputable job platform someone writes to you as a project director. Your profile names your employer.
steps.message: Hi! Your profile is a perfect fit for a role with us. Very good salary, fully remote. Would you have time this week for a short talk with our HR team?
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Agree, a conversation cannot hurt
options.feedback: The bait is taken. In the first video call the supposed HR person even shares an account with private photos and videos, to win your trust.

options.label: Tell the security team: whoever approaches you because of your employer may mean exactly that employer
options.feedback: Strong. Binance reported 57 foiled cases in 2026 that it suspects are linked to North Korea. Only reports make such patterns visible.

steps.narration: Round two: you talk through a well-known chat app with the supposed CEO of a company. Shortly before the end comes the task.
steps.message:
One last thing, a small coding assignment. Download the repository and get it running, then we will look at it together.
repo.test/hiring/assignment
steps.question: Your work computer is right in front of you. What do you do?

options.label: Download it to the work computer and set it up
options.feedback: This is the moment. Malicious code already runs during setup, and endpoint protection does not detect it. From now on the attackers have your computer.

options.label: Only read the code, and run it in an isolated environment without company access
options.feedback: Good. Foreign code must never go where your access lives. Ideally you report the whole thing as well.

options.label: Stop and report it to the security team
options.feedback: Right. Real companies have no problem with that. A job interview is no reason for foreign code on a work computer.

timeline.what: While setting up an AI tool, a wallet DevOps engineer downloads a tampered Homebrew installer. Binance detects and removes it and rotates credentials as a precaution. By then the attackers already know who looks after the wallets.
A software engineer is approached through a job platform and goes through two fake interviews. The "assignment" puts previously unseen malware on his work computer.
Through this computer and an internal AI tool, the attackers take over the computers of two more staff members and find a token with deployment rights.
In under three hours they use the stolen access and the internal wallet signing service: transactions bypass the normal withdrawal process, and about 6.3 billion US dollars are gone.

Withdrawals stop for about 48 hours. According to Binance, 98% of the affected token assets are replenished by 31 October. By 3 November about 2.85 billion has been frozen or intercepted. The FBI attributes the theft to North Korea.

lesson: The most expensive attack in crypto history needed two people doing something normal: looking for a tool and applying for a job. Foreign software and foreign code never belong on a computer with company access, and a tempting job offer is worth a report.

title: One call, one new password, 300 million pounds
summary: In April 2025 attackers posed as one of the 50,000 people working for Marks & Spencer and got an outside service provider to reset a password. The damage: about 300 million pounds of operating profit.
disclaimer: Interactive reconstruction: the conversation is illustrative, its wording is not public. The facts come from the chairman's hearing before the UK Parliament, as relayed by BleepingComputer, Infosecurity Magazine and Insurance Journal. Media name a particular service provider. M&S did not, and neither does this case.

steps.narration: You work on the help desk of a service provider for a large retailer. A call comes in.
steps.message: Hello, I am locked out of my account and I have to finish the stock planning today. Could you quickly reset my password? I can give you my name and staff number.
steps.question: Name and staff number match the system. What do you do?

options.label: Reset the password, the details are correct
options.feedback: That was the door. A name and a staff number can be found out. The chairman later simply called it impersonation.

options.label: Verify the identity a second way: call back on the number on file, or get the manager to confirm
options.feedback: Exactly. Knowledge that others can have proves nothing. A call back takes two minutes.

steps.narration: The caller grows impatient and follows up in writing.
steps.message: This is taking too long. Everything has stopped here. Shall I call your manager and say it is down to you?
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Give in, I do not want any trouble
options.feedback: Pressure is part of the craft: that is exactly why the process must hold under pressure too.

options.label: Stay friendly, stick to the procedure and report the case
options.feedback: Strong. Whoever is real can wait two minutes. Whoever pushes has a reason.

timeline.what: According to chairman Archie Norman, the break-in begins with impersonation: the attackers pose as one of the 50,000 people working for M&S and get a third party to reset a password.
M&S detects the intrusion. The company shuts systems down itself to stop the spread. Among other things, this hits online shopping for weeks.
Norman testifies before the UK Parliament. He confirms the ransomware group DragonForce, but leaves open whether a ransom was paid.
M&S expects about 300 million pounds less operating profit and hopes to recover a substantial part through insurance.

lesson: No virus and no vulnerability, just a convincing conversation. The help desk is one of a company's most important security controls, including at a service provider. Passwords are reset only after a real check.

title: When the slot machines went dark
summary: In September 2023 a social engineering attack crippled parts of MGM Resorts' casinos in Las Vegas: slot machines, room bookings and card payments. The cost: at least 100 million US dollars.
disclaimer: Interactive reconstruction: the conversation is illustrative. MGM speaks of a social engineering attack by criminal third parties, but has not disclosed the exact entry point. The often cited help desk call rests on media and vendor reports and is not officially confirmed.

steps.narration: You work on the IT help desk of a large hotel and casino group. On the phone is someone introducing himself as a colleague. His name can also be found online, on professional networks.
steps.message: Hi, I cannot get into my account and the phone with the app is gone. Could you set up new access for me? I am sitting in the hotel and urgently need to get in.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Set up access and reset the second factor, he knows all the details
options.feedback: Such groups work mainly by phone and text. A reset account is all they need to get in.

options.label: Verify the identity through the defined route, for instance through the manager or in person
options.feedback: Exactly. A lost phone is the most common story. That is exactly when the full check applies.

steps.narration: Somewhat later, an unusual notice reaches you.
steps.message: Monitoring: new admin account created. Sign-ins from an unknown location. Ticket automatically rated low.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Rated low, I will look at it after the weekend
options.feedback: Soon the machines and booking systems stand still. Every hour of head start counts for the attackers.

options.label: Alert the security team immediately
options.feedback: Right. Better once too often. Reported early means less damage.

timeline.what: The attack disrupts casino operations, room bookings and card payments at sites in Las Vegas. The group Scattered Spider, known for phone and text phishing, claims responsibility. MGM does not confirm details about ransomware.

MGM reports costs of at least 100 million US dollars to the US securities regulator and expects insurance to cover them. Customers' personal data was stolen, in some cases including Social Security and passport numbers.
Systems are restored. According to its CEO, the group plans up to 40 million US dollars of additional IT investment.

lesson: A multi-billion group with modern technology was attacked through people. Whoever resets access needs a procedure that also holds when the caller is nice, stressed and well informed.

title: A text, a call, and all the codes at once
summary: In August 2023 a single employee at Retool fell for a text message. A call with a faked voice got the last code, and cloud sync delivered the rest: 27 customers from the crypto industry were affected.
disclaimer: Interactive reconstruction: the messages are illustrative. The facts come from Retool's report as relayed by Help Net Security and BleepingComputer. The link to the theft at Fortress Trust rests on media reports and was not confirmed by Retool.

steps.narration: Your company is moving its logins to Okta, as announced. A text arrives, supposedly from IT.
steps.message: IT: A problem with your account is preventing your migration from finishing. Please check here: portal-sso.test/migration
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Open the link and sign in, the migration really is happening
options.feedback: The page looks like your login portal and now has your password. Several colleagues got the text, only one clicked: one was enough.

options.label: Open the portal myself through my bookmark and report the text to IT
options.feedback: Right. The real migration makes the bait believable, not the link.

steps.narration: Shortly afterwards someone calls. The person sounds exactly like someone from your team and knows internal procedures.
steps.message: Hi, IT here. For your migration I just need one more code from your authenticator app, then you are done.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Give the code, I know the voice after all
options.feedback: With this code the attacker adds his own device to your Okta account. According to Retool, the voice was a deepfake.

options.label: Hang up and call IT myself through the known route
options.feedback: Exactly. You pass a code to nobody, not even to a familiar voice.

steps.narration: Your authenticator app offers to back up all your codes in your Google account.
steps.message:
Back up codes to your account?
That way you never lose them, not even with a new phone.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Of course, that is practical
options.feedback: At Retool this gave the attacker all codes at once through the Google account. The second factor became the same factor.

options.label: Rather use a hardware security key or passkey where possible
options.feedback: Strong. These methods tie the sign-in to the real site. A code can be talked out of you by phone, a key cannot.

timeline.what: Several employees get text messages that look like they come from IT, during the move to Okta. One person falls for the fake login page.
A caller poses as IT, according to Retool with a faked voice, and gets one more code. The attacker adds his own device and reaches all the account's codes through Google sync.

Through internal tools, 27 cloud customers from the crypto industry are affected, but not customers with their own installation. Media link the incident to a loss of nearly 15 million US dollars at Fortress Trust.
Retool makes the incident public. According to Google, users can choose whether codes are synced, and Google recommends FIDO methods.

lesson: Real occasions make the best bait. Retool's conclusion: even with perfect training, mistakes happen. That is why you need both: people who report, and sign-in methods that cannot be talked out of you by phone.

title: The phone call that cost 130 accounts
summary: In July 2020 attackers made targeted phone calls to Twitter employees. Using the access obtained this way, they reached internal tools and hijacked prominent accounts for a bitcoin scam.
disclaimer: Interactive reconstruction: the conversation is illustrative. The facts in the timeline come from Twitter's updates and the New York financial regulator's report.

steps.narration: You are working from home, and the pandemic has been going on for months. Your phone rings.
steps.message: "Hello, this is IT. We are switching the VPN over and we see a problem on your side. Please sign in briefly on our site and I will guide you through."
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Sign in, the colleague sounds competent
options.feedback: The call sounds real, the site looks like the VPN portal. Your login details are gone.

options.label: Hang up and call IT on the known number
options.feedback: That is the one action that stops this attack.

options.label: Ask for a ticket number
options.feedback: Good reaction, but only a callback on the known number really gives you certainty.

steps.narration: A colleague messages you: she got a similar call.
steps.message: "Hey, did IT call you about the VPN too? That was odd, wasn't it?"
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Both of you inform the security team
options.feedback: Two identical calls are a pattern. That is exactly what the security team needs right away.

options.label: Wait and see, it will be nothing
options.feedback: The attackers needed only a few people to get further.

timeline.what: Using phone spear phishing, the perpetrators obtain employees' access, including to internal support tools.
130 accounts are targeted, and tweets are sent from 45 of them: "I will double your bitcoin".
The perpetrators take over 100,000 US dollars in bitcoin and are later arrested.

lesson: No zero-day, no malware: just a convincing call. Calling back on the known number is the strongest defence against vishing.
sources: Twitter: updates on the security incident, July 2020
New York State Department of Financial Services: investigation report, October 2020

title: Worn down by push notifications
summary: In September 2022 an attacker broke into Uber. He knew an external contractor's password and kept sending 2FA requests until one of them was approved.
disclaimer: Interactive reconstruction: the messages are illustrative. The facts in the timeline come from Uber's statement and media reports.

steps.narration: It is late in the evening. Your phone keeps vibrating.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Approve so it finally stops
options.feedback: That is exactly what MFA fatigue aims for. The door is open.

options.label: Deny and inform IT right away
options.feedback: Right. The requests prove your password is known. It must be changed right away.

options.label: Mute the phone and go to sleep
options.feedback: You approved nothing, but nobody learns that someone has your password. The attacker will try again tomorrow.

steps.narration: Shortly afterwards someone contacts you by messenger.
steps.message: "Hi, this is Uber IT. About those requests: please approve the next one and it will stop right away."
steps.question: What do you do?

options.label: Approve the next request
options.feedback: Real IT never asks you to approve a sign-in you did not start yourself.

options.label: Call back through the official hotline
options.feedback: Switching channels exposes the attacker.

timeline.what: According to Uber, the external contractor's password was probably bought on the dark web after his device was infected with malware.
The attacker repeatedly tries to sign in. The requests are denied at first, and finally one is approved. According to media reports, he also contacted the contractor by messenger, posing as IT.
He gains access to further employee accounts and internal tools and posts in the company chat. Uber informs the authorities.

lesson: 2FA only protects you if nobody is pressured into approving it. Requests you did not start: deny and report.
sources: Media reports on the incident, September 2022
